summary: Uses CBOR's tag mechanism to define tags for typed arrays of numbers, such as arrays of fixed-size integers or floating-point values. It also adds tags for multi-dimensional and homogeneous arrays, so bulk numeric data can be stored compactly.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of writing numbers one by one with labels, you put a sticker on a whole tray saying all the items inside are the same kind. That makes packing them much smaller.

questions: how to encode typed arrays in cbor
what are cbor tags for numeric arrays
what are cbor typed array tags
what is cbor tag 41 homogeneous array
subtitle: CBOR tags that label a whole block of same-type numbers, so arrays of integers or floats can be shipped without re-encoding each one.

tldr.problem: Sending a large array of numbers in plain CBOR means converting each number one by one and paying for a type on every element, even though the data often already sits in memory as a typed array.
tldr.mechanism: A single tag in the range 64 to 87 wraps one CBOR byte string and says what kind of number it holds (integer or float, signed or not, big or little endian, 8 to 128 bits). Extra tags describe multi-dimensional and homogeneous arrays.
tldr.outcome: The tags are registered with IANA using this document as the reference, so encoders can send numeric buffers directly. Encoders have wide freedom in choosing variants, so protocols that need deterministic encoding must pick one.

today: RFC 8746 is a Standards Track document with Proposed Standard status, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the reference for the IANA registration of these tags.

sections.title: Why Typed Arrays in CBOR
sections.content:
The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR, defined in RFC 7049) carries structured data without a pre-agreed schema, and it can be extended through a tag registry kept by IANA. This document uses that mechanism to define tags for typed arrays of numbers, a form that is in use in the Web graphics community and in JavaScript.

Typed arrays can carry a lot of data. The goal is to interchange them in CBOR without converting each number in the array, and to save the space that would go into encoding a type for every element. The document also adds tags for multi-dimensional and homogeneous arrays, and it is meant as the reference document for the IANA registration of all these tags.

An application has considerable freedom: it can choose endianness, signed or unsigned, bits per element, or skip these tags and use more basic CBOR. There is no 'preferred' representation, so a protocol that wants deterministic encoding has to say which variants it uses for each case.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs often hold long lists of numbers all of the same kind. This RFC gives a way to label the whole list once, instead of labeling every number, so the message is smaller and faster to build.

sections.title: Typed Arrays and Number Types
sections.content:
A typed array is a homogeneous array of numbers that are all encoded in one binary form. The concatenation of those representations is placed in a single CBOR byte string (major type 2), and one tag in front of it says what the numbers are.

Three classes of numbers are covered: unsigned integers (uint), signed integers in two's complement (sint) and IEEE 754 binary floating point numbers, which are always signed. Each class comes in four lengths, selected by a value ll from 0 to 3: 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits for integers, and binary16, binary32, binary64 and binary128 for floats.

Because the point is to ship the underlying buffers as they are, and those may be big endian (network byte order) or little endian, both byte orders need tags. In total that makes 24 variants.
sections.plainLanguage: There are whole numbers and decimal numbers, small boxes and big boxes, and two ways of writing a number's bytes forwards or backwards. Each combination gets its own sticker.

sections.title: How the Tag Number Encodes the Type
sections.content:
The 24 tags occupy tag values 64 to 87, laid out so that all the information can be read from the bits of the tag. The low 8 bits are split into the constant bits 0b010, then f (0 for integer, 1 for float), s (1 for signed integer, 0 for float or unsigned), e (0 for big endian, 1 for little endian) and ll (the length value).

The number of bytes in each element is 2**(f + ll). The array does not carry an element count. The count is implied by the byte string length and computed as bytelength >> (f + ll).

There are special cases. For 8-bit integers endianness is meaningless, so only the big-endian tag is used. The tag for little-endian sint8 (76) MUST NOT be used and is reserved. The tag that would mean little-endian uint8 (68) instead means a uint8 array using clamped conversion, matching the JavaScript ToUint8Clamp behaviour, so such arrays can round-trip through CBOR. Floats are always signed, so the tag values 88 to 95 remain free for other specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker number is a little code. Each bit of it answers one question, such as whole or decimal, or which way round the bytes go. A reader can work out the tray's contents just from the number.

sections.title: Multi-dimensional and Homogeneous Arrays
sections.content:
Three more tags are defined. The multi-dimensional array tag 40 wraps an array of two arrays: the first lists the dimensions (unsigned integers distinct from zero, from the outer dimension to the inner one), the second holds the contents. The contents can be a classical CBOR array, a typed array or a homogeneous array. If they are a typed array, the element type of the whole structure is that of the typed array. In tag 40 the last dimension is contiguous (row-major order).

Tag 1040 is the same except that the first dimension is contiguous (column-major order). Row-major order is the preferred order for this specification, and the column-major tag was taken from a different number space (the first come first served space) to make that preference evident.

The homogeneous array tag 41 marks a classical CBOR array as having elements that are all of the same application data type. The element type is determined by the application type of the first element. It can help application data models that give special meaning to such arrays, and decoders in strongly typed languages may create native homogeneous arrays instead of ordered lists. Applying it to a typed array would be redundant, so that is not provided.
sections.plainLanguage: A tray of numbers can be shaped like a grid, and the sticker says how wide and tall the grid is and whether you read it row by row or column by column. Another sticker just says that everything in a plain list is the same kind of thing.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows a C declaration uint16_t a[2][3] with rows {2, 4, 8} and {4, 16, 256}. In CBOR it becomes tag 40 around an array of two items: the dimensions [2, 3] and a tag 65 (uint16, big endian) byte string of 12 bytes holding the six values.

The same grid can instead use tag 40 with a basic CBOR array of six numbers, which happens to be shorter here because the numbers are small. With tag 1040 the six values are listed in column-major order: 2, 4, 4, 16, 8, 256.

For homogeneous arrays the RFC gives a C++ array of two booleans, encoded under tag 41 as true, false, and a second example of an array of structures with a boolean and an integer in each element.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same little grid of six numbers packed three ways: as a labeled tray, as a plain list with a grid label, and read column by column.

sections.title: CDDL Names and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
For use with the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL, RFC 8610), the RFC recommends type names such as ta-uint16be = #6.65(bstr), ta-float32le = #6.85(bstr), homogeneous<array> = #6.41(array) and multi-dim<dim, array> = #6.40([dim, array]).

IANA has allocated the tags with this document as the specification reference. They come from the 'specification required' space (24 to 255), except 1040, which comes from the 'first come first served' space (256 and up). Tag 76 is listed as reserved for a future revision of typed array tags.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also hands out short nicknames for each sticker, and the official keeper of the numbers writes them in the public list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7049 apply. The homogeneous array tag makes a promise about its contents that a maliciously built input may break. A decoder therefore must not be driven into an undefined state by elements that do not keep the promise, and it must keep meeting its API contract.

As with any interchange format, an attacker may control the shape of the data, so the application needs to validate it. Typed arrays add one point: an attacker might substitute a Uint8ClampedArray where a Uint8Array is expected, or the other way round, which could lead to very different processing. Applications that could be affected need to be careful about this distinction in input validation.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sends you a tray labeled 'all apples' with a pear hidden in it, your program should not crash. It should check what it really got.

data.title: uint16_t a[2][3] in CBOR
data.code:
<Tag 40> # multi-dimensional array tag
   82       # array(2)
     82      # array(2)
       02     # unsigned(2) 1st Dimension
       03     # unsigned(3) 2nd Dimension
     <Tag 65> # uint16 array
       4c     # byte string(12)
         0002 0004 0008 0004 0010 0100
